passage: Six months after Vidya began teaching in Kalyanpur, the two of them sat on the roof of the village house with a notebook and a flask of tea. "What got better?" Harish asked, pen ready. "The school, the pay, the pride of it," said Vidya. "And what hurt?" "The long weekends apart, and the bus. Three hours each way, and I arrive tired for you." Harish wrote both down. Neither suggested going back. "What if I find a room in Sundarpur? It's only forty minutes by bike from there. And we fix which weekends I come home, and which you come to me." Harish thought of the mango grove and the tractor repairs, and nodded. "Every second weekend, each way. And a call on Wednesdays." They wrote the new plan under the old one, and it looked like a plan, not an apology.

qa.q: What did Vidya say hurt about the arrangement?
qa.a: The long weekends apart and the three-hour bus each way.

qa.q: How does Vidya feel about the job and about the distance?
qa.a: Vidya feels proud of the school and the pay, but tired and sad about the time apart, as arriving tired for Harish shows.

qa.q: What could they do if the new arrangement also strains them?
qa.a: They could review it again after a set time and adjust the weekends or the calls, rather than dropping the job.

qa.q: How might Harish see the change to the plan?
qa.a: Harish may feel relieved that going back is not the only answer, and glad that the work in the grove and with the tractor was considered.

grounding: At the six-month review, Vidya and Harish note what improved and what hurt, and adjust with a nearer room and a visit schedule instead of reversing everything.

passage:
Six months after Santiago started his job in Gothenburg and Anders stayed in Stockholm, they sat in their kitchen with the list they'd made in the spring.
"What's better?" Anders asked.
"My work," Santiago said. "Honestly, it's what I hoped. And your promotion happened because you stayed."
"And what hurts?"
Santiago didn't hesitate. "The weekends. Two nights a week together isn't enough. And the Sunday train back makes me miserable."
Anders nodded. "I dread Sundays too."
They didn't talk about quitting. Instead they looked for smaller changes. Santiago's company had an office in Norrköping, halfway between. He'd ask to work from there two days a week. They'd also set a visit schedule: Anders would come to Gothenburg every second weekend, so Santiago wasn't always the one travelling.
"We're not undoing it," Anders said. "We're fixing the part that hurts."

qa.q: Which town's office was halfway between?
How did Santiago feel about the weekends apart?
qa.a: Santiago felt miserable, especially on the Sunday train back, finding two nights a week together not enough.

qa.q: What else could Anders and Santiago add to their adjustments?
qa.a: They could set another review in a few months to check whether the halfway office and visits are actually helping.

qa.q: How does the review look from Anders's side?
qa.a: Anders shares the dread of Sundays and prefers adjusting the arrangement rather than reversing it, since Anders's own promotion came from staying.

grounding: It shows a couple at a six-month review noting what improved and what hurt, and adjusting with a shorter commute and a visit schedule rather than reversing everything.

The review happened in the family room of the hospital in Pune where Nandini worked, because it was the only quiet place either of them could get to on a Tuesday.
Six months earlier, Asif had taken the job in Mumbai while Nandini stayed. They'd promised a proper review.
Nandini had a notebook. "Good things first."
"My job is great. Your fellowship is on track. The money's better."
"Hard things?"
Asif rubbed his face. "The weekends. I get in on Friday night, exhausted, and leave Sunday afternoon. We spend half of it just catching up. It hurts."
"For me too," Nandini said. "I feel like a visitor in my own marriage."
They didn't undo the move. Instead, Asif asked his manager about working from Pune every Monday, making weekends three nights instead of two. And Nandini would come to Mumbai one weekend a month.
She wrote the new plan in her notebook and underlined "review again in March".

qa.a: In the family room of the hospital in Pune where Nandini worked.

qa.q: What did Nandini mean by feeling like a visitor in her own marriage?
qa.a: Nandini felt hurt and lonely, since the short weekends made their time together feel rushed, like a visit rather than a shared life.

qa.q: What else could Nandini and Asif do before the March review?
qa.a: They could keep short notes on what helps and what still hurts, so the next review is honest and specific.

qa.q: How might Asif experience the new plan?
qa.a: Asif gets longer weekends and fewer exhausting trips, so he may feel relieved and more connected to Nandini.

grounding: It shows a couple at a six-month review noting what improved and what hurt, and adjusting with a shorter commute and visit schedule instead of reversing the move.
